name: Garnet
workload: RESP-translated YCSB-A workload, 256M 8-byte keys, string values 8B-several KB, using memtier_benchmark and Garnet's own Resp.bench load generator against Garnet/Valkey/KeyDB/Dragonfly on Azure Standard F72s_v2 VMs (72 vCPUs, 144GB RAM), Ubuntu 24.04, accelerated TCP networking
claimed_speedup: Table 1 (normalized to Redis): node throughput 108x, P99 latency at batch size 16 down to 0.25x; memtier GET throughput >=20x higher and P99 latency 3x lower than Valkey at high client load; up to 40x/6x higher throughput than KeyDB/Dragonfly in some GET experiments; checkpoint speed 257x, scale-out (migration) speed 94x vs Redis
hardware: Azure Standard F72s_v2 VMs, 72 vCPUs, 144GB RAM, Ubuntu 24.04 with accelerated TCP networking
stars_or_usage: 12k stars; described as widely deployed inside Microsoft
tradeoffs: Runs on the .NET runtime (GC, JIT) rather than being a native binary; kernel-bypass networking (eRPC/DPDK path) used for the best latency numbers is a prototype not shipped in the open-source build; complex RESP data types (SortedSet, HyperLogLog) add overhead
caveats: Evaluation performed and published by Garnet's own authors (Microsoft Research + Facebook/Meta-adjacent academics via VLDB peer review), not a fully independent third party, though it is peer-reviewed (PVLDB 19(2):224-237) with full hardware/workload disclosure; memtier_benchmark itself became client-bottlenecked at high throughput so most headline figures use Garnet's own Resp.bench tool instead
found_via: GitHub: microsoft/FASTER README (deprecated, points to Garnet as successor) -> gh api repos/microsoft/garnet; VLDB paper fetched via WebFetch from https://badrish.net/papers/garnet-vldb2026.pdf and read as PDF

name: Caffeine
workload: JMH microbenchmark (ComputeBenchmark/GetPutBenchmark) at 16 threads, varying read/write mixes (100% read, 75/25 read/write, 100% write) on a bounded in-process cache, vs ConcurrentLinkedHashMap, Guava Cache, Ehcache, Infinispan and plain ConcurrentHashMap
claimed_speedup: server-class (Xeon E5-2698B v3, 16 threads): 100% read 382.4M ops/s vs 313.9M (ConcurrentLinkedHashMap, ~1.2x) and 43.1M (Guava, ~8.9x); 75/25 read/write 279.4M vs 122.3M (~2.3x) and 37.3M (Guava, ~7.5x); 100% write 48.3M vs 39.8M (~1.2x)
hardware: Server-class: single-socket Xeon E5-2698B v3 @ 2.00GHz, 16 cores (hyperthreading disabled), 224GB RAM, Ubuntu 15.04, Azure G4 instance; desktop-class: MacBook Pro i7-4870HQ @ 2.50GHz
stars_or_usage: 17.9k stars; used as the cache implementation inside Spring, Cassandra, Solr and others
tradeoffs: In-process JVM cache, not a distributed/remote cache like Redis or Memcached, so it solves a different deployment problem (per-process hit ratio and speed rather than shared/networked state); W-TinyLFU admission policy adds bookkeeping vs a plain LRU
caveats: CPU model and OS are stated but the exact JVM version/flags used for the JMH run are not given in the wiki page as fetched; benchmark code and harness are public in the repo (ComputeBenchmark.java, GetPutBenchmark.java) which is why this is scored B rather than C
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos --topic cache --language c++ did not surface this; found via reasoning about 'LRU baselines the benchmark names' + gh api repos/ben-manes/caffeine, then WebFetch of the Benchmarks wiki page

name: Pelikan / Segcache
workload: NSDI'21 paper evaluation of Segcache (Pelikan's TTL-segmented storage engine) on production-derived cache workloads, scaling to 24 threads, comparing per-object metadata overhead and multi-core throughput scaling vs Memcached's slab allocator
claimed_speedup: ~8x higher throughput than Memcached at 24 threads; 5 bytes/object metadata vs Memcached's 56 bytes, cutting cache memory requirements 22-60% vs other state-of-the-art designs and 40-90% vs Pelikan's own prior slab storage
stars_or_usage: 295 stars (current Rust rewrite); legacy C implementation at github.com/twitter/pelikan has ~2k stars
tradeoffs: TTL-segmented design trades some flexibility (object grouping by expiry) for memory efficiency; original Segcache/legacy Pelikan was C, current pelikan-io/pelikan is a full Rust rewrite so the exact peer-reviewed binary is not what ships today
caveats: Numbers are quoted from the project's own blog restating its peer-reviewed NSDI'21 paper; did not obtain the paper PDF directly in this session to confirm exact hardware/CPU model and compiler flags used in the formal evaluation, so this is capped at Tier B rather than A
found_via: GitHub: gh api repos/pelikan-io/pelikan; README opened directly, linking to Segcache blog and NSDI'21 paper page

name: Pogocache
workload: memtier_benchmark 100K SET + 100K GET ops per client, 256 clients over 16 I/O threads, pipelining 1/10/25/50, on AWS c8g.8xlarge (32-core ARM64), Unix socket, persistence off, 31 runs per point (median reported)
claimed_speedup: throughput ranking (pipeline 1, 8 threads): pogocache 3,145,960 ops/s vs memcache 2,601,306, garnet 1,548,050, dragonfly 1,407,584, valkey 1,331,683, redis 909,837 (~3.5x Redis, ~1.2x Memcached); lowest latency (111us) and fewest CPU cycles/op (6968) of the group
hardware: AWS c8g.8xlarge, 32-core non-NUMA ARM64
tradeoffs: Newer/less battle-tested than Redis/Memcached in production; supports Memcache, RESP and Postgres wire protocols but not full Redis command set (data structures, scripting, etc.)
caveats: The cache-benchmarks suite comparing pogocache to Redis/Valkey/Dragonfly/Garnet/Memcache is written and run by pogocache's own author (tidwall), so it is not a fully independent third party, even though the methodology (31 runs, median, stated hardware, stated versions) is unusually rigorous; exact compiler/build flags for each server are not listed, only released versions/commits
found_via: GitHub: gh api repos/tidwall/pogocache; README table pointing to linked cache-benchmarks repo, opened directly

name: Dragonfly
workload: memtier_benchmark SET/GET ops (-d 256) against Redis on m5.large/m5.xlarge, and against Memcached on c6gn.16xlarge; also idle/peak memory usage during BGSAVE-equivalent snapshot
claimed_speedup: up to 25x throughput vs a single Redis process on c6gn.16xlarge (3.8M QPS); ~4.8x SET QPS vs Memcached (3844K vs 806K) on c6gn.16xlarge; ~30% more memory efficient than Redis at idle
hardware: AWS m5.large, m5.xlarge, c6gn.16xlarge, r6g/c7g (instance types stated; CPU model not stated)
tradeoffs: Business Source License restricts running it as a competing hosted service (converts to Apache-2.0 on 2030-11-01); single shared-nothing multi-threaded architecture differs operationally from Redis single-thread model
caveats: First-party README benchmark; AWS instance type given but exact CPU model, compiler, and build flags are not stated, so numbers cannot be independently reproduced from the README alone. A separate independent-ish suite (tidwall/cache-benchmarks) corroborates Dragonfly beating Redis/Memcached on AWS c8g.8xlarge with stated versions (see the Pogocache entry in this file).
found_via: GitHub: gh api repos/dragonflydb/dragonfly (seeded from prior knowledge of 'modern replacement for Redis and Memcached'); README benchmarks section opened directly

name: IKV (Inlined Key-Value Store)
workload: Multi-threaded client issuing blocking GET calls at fixed QPS levels (25K/50K/100K) against IKV (embedded, in-process) vs a 16-shard Redis Cluster on AWS ElastiCache; measuring avg/p50/p99 response time in microseconds
claimed_speedup: at 100K QPS: IKV avg 3.13us/p50 2.89us/p99 5.65us vs Redis Cluster avg 319us/p50 305us/p99 514us (roughly 100x lower average latency); README also claims embedded local Flash/SSD-backed IKV is still ~2x faster than an all-in-memory remote Redis cluster
tradeoffs: IKV is an embedded/in-process library colocated with the application (no network hop) rather than a shared remote cache, so much of the 100x gap is network round-trip elimination rather than a faster core engine; eventual consistency instead of Redis's stronger read-after-write guarantees; requires a separate data-plane (streams/object storage) to keep embedded replicas in sync
caveats: First-party README claim; linked full report is a Google Doc that could not be fully read in this session (only its title, 'IKV Perf Benchmarks | A comparison with Redis', was visible), so hardware/CPU model and compiler flags are unconfirmed; comparing an embedded cache against a networked cache is not entirely apples-to-apples for a 'faster engine' claim, though it is a legitimate real-workload latency win for the intended use case (ML feature serving)
found_via: HN Algolia: query 'faster than redis' -> 'IKV: embedded key-value store, 100x faster than Redis' (github.com/inlinedio/ikv-store); repo README opened directly

name: KeyDB
workload: memtier_benchmark, 32 threads over TLS, standard Redis GET/SET ops; benchmark client on AWS m5.8xlarge (32 cores), database instances on m5.4xlarge
claimed_speedup: over 7x faster than Redis with TLS enabled (~1M ops/s at 16 KeyDB threads vs ~130k ops/s for Redis 6 with TLS); Redis loses 36% throughput enabling TLS (61% with io-threads+TLS) while KeyDB shows almost no decline
hardware: AWS m5.8xlarge (client, 32 cores), m5.4xlarge (server instances) — CPU model not stated
tradeoffs: Multithreading changes the concurrency/atomicity model vs Redis (MVCC-style access under a global lock for KEYS/SCAN); staying in sync with upstream Redis features is ongoing maintenance burden for a fork
caveats: First-party blog benchmark (KeyDB's own team); AWS instance type stated but not exact CPU model, compiler, or build flags; repository has had no commits in ~2.5 years even though the fork's changes are still substantive vs upstream Redis
found_via: GitHub: gh api repos/Snapchat/KeyDB (seeded from prior knowledge of 'multithreaded fork of Redis'); README benchmark link opened directly

name: Bodo DataFrames
language: Python (JIT-compiled to native code via an MPI-based C++ runtime)
workload: NYC Taxi FHVHV benchmark: 1.03B-row / 24-column Parquet dataset (24.7 GiB) joined with a small weather CSV, average-trip-duration/count aggregation; single-node run on one AWS r6i.16xlarge (32 physical cores, 512 GiB RAM)
claimed_speedup: single node: Bodo 27.71s vs Polars 1.25.2 at 282.34s (~10.2x faster) and vs Daft 0.4.7 at 69.59s (~2.5x faster); 4-node cluster: Bodo 17s vs PySpark 3.5.2 at 389s (20x), Dask at 915s (50x), Modin+Ray at 4155s (250x) (derived from page data)
hardware: AWS EC2 r6i.16xlarge (32 physical cores, 512 GiB RAM); cluster variant uses 4x r6i.16xlarge
tradeoffs: Drop-in pandas-API replacement but relies on JIT compilation and MPI for parallelism; the Bodo Platform build used for the cluster run links a forked version of Arrow for faster Parquet reads (bodo-ai/arrow-cpp-feedstock), a deviation from stock Apache Arrow
caveats: First-party benchmark (Bodo's own repo), not an independent suite; numbers are read from bar-chart PNGs rather than a raw results table; single-node comparison excludes pandas directly (pandas cannot practically process this dataset on one machine); results are dated snapshots (Dec 2024 / Mar 2025) of specific package versions
found_via: GitHub: gh api repos/bodo-ai/bodo (README benchmarks section)

name: chDB
workload: ClickBench 'DataFrame' comparison view (43 analytical queries over the hits dataset), chDB vs Pandas vs Polars vs DuckDB, all run in DataFrame mode on AWS c6a.metal (500GB gp2)
claimed_speedup: aggregate relative time across all queries: chDB 1.35x vs Pandas 71.18x and Polars 9.99x (best-per-query = 1.00x) -> chDB is roughly 53x faster than Pandas and 7.4x faster than Polars in this comparison, and about on par with DuckDB (1.35x vs 1.40x) (derived from page data)

caveats: Numbers read from a screenshot table embedded in the README, generated from the live, JS-rendered benchmark.clickhouse.com page (which this session could not render directly); the 'beats DuckDB' part of the claim (1.35x vs 1.40x) is marginal/within noise, unlike the large, clear wins over Pandas and Polars

claimed_speedup: sum of best-of-3 times across all 43 ClickBench queries: 7.41s for Umbra vs 18.03s for ClickHouse (~2.4x faster) and vs 26.25s for DuckDB (~3.5x faster), with 0 failed queries (derived from page data)

name: Velox
workload: ClickBench: 43 analytical SQL queries over the ~100M-row 'hits' table (single Parquet file, queried in place), single-node AWS c6a.xlarge, driven through Meta's Axiom SQL layer on top of the Velox execution engine
claimed_speedup: best case ~2.3x faster than ClickHouse on one query (Q33: 10.49s vs 17.57s) and 1.5-1.8x faster on three others, but slower overall: sum of best-of-3 times across all 43 queries is 214.09s for Velox/Axiom vs 124.35s for ClickHouse, and far slower (>100x) on several count-style queries (derived from page data)
compiler_and_flags: CMake Release build on Ubuntu 24.04 with default toolchain (-DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release); no explicit compiler name/version or optimization flags beyond that stated
hardware: AWS EC2 c6a.xlarge, single node
tradeoffs: Velox itself is only a C++ execution-engine library with no SQL parser/optimizer/catalog; this result actually benchmarks facebookincubator/axiom (a thin SQL layer built on Velox); must be built from source (no release binaries), which is memory- and time-intensive
caveats: Mixed/weak result: wins on a handful of queries by 1.5-2.3x but is ~1.7x slower in aggregate and drastically slower on several queries; ClickBench's own README is openly hostile to the Velox paper ('a dishonest academic paper'); included here for the documented per-query wins, not as an overall 'faster than ClickHouse' claim
found_via: GitHub: ClickHouse/ClickBench shootout repo (gh api repos/ClickHouse/ClickBench/contents/velox)

name: Sirius
workload: TPC-H benchmark (22 queries) hot runs at scale factors SF100/300/500/1000 (100GB-1TB), Sirius (a GPU execution engine plugged into DuckDB via Substrait) vs plain DuckDB on CPU
claimed_speedup: 5.5x faster at SF100 (1.71s vs 9.37s), 5.7x at SF300 (4.48s vs 25.72s), 5.2x at SF500 (8.14s vs 42.25s), 2.7x at SF1000 (31.79s vs 85.91s); also 2.1x-5.3x cheaper per run
benchmark_url: https://github.com/sirius-db/sirius (README performance chart; image at docs/super-sirius-perf.png)
hardware: Sirius (GPU): AWS g7e.2xl/4xl/8xl instances, NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 96GB; DuckDB (CPU) v1.5.5: AWS Graviton5 m9g.16xlarge
tradeoffs: Requires an NVIDIA GPU (Turing+, CUDA 12.x/13.x) and Linux with io_uring enabled; plugs into DuckDB via Substrait and falls back silently to CPU for unsupported operators; only DuckDB is a supported target today (StarRocks integration planned)
caveats: First-party benchmark; numbers were read from a bar chart PNG in the README, not a raw results table; no compiler/build flags stated; the speedup margin shrinks as scale grows (5.5x at SF100 down to 2.7x at SF1000), suggesting GPU memory/bandwidth becomes the bottleneck at larger sizes
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "sirius GPU DuckDB"; gh api repos/sirius-db/sirius

name: DobLIX
workload: SOSD real-world (WIKI, AMZN, FB, OSM) and synthetic (LOGN, UNI) datasets, 64M 8-byte-key/64-byte-value pairs, YCSB-style read/write workloads on RocksDB 8.1.1
claimed_speedup: Up to 2.21x higher read throughput vs RocksDB indexing; up to 2.67x better throughput vs TridentKV/Bourbon/RocksDB combined; 81% higher throughput than RocksDB with larger caches; 1.19x-2.21x over state-of-the-art learned-index baselines within RocksDB
hardware: 64-core AMD Ryzen Threadripter Pro 5995WX (2.7GHz), 256GB DDR4 RAM, Samsung 980 Pro 2TB NVMe SSD, Ubuntu 20.04
license: BSD-3-Clause (inherited RocksDB LICENSE; repo built as a modified RocksDB tree, GitHub shows NOASSERTION due to mixed files but LICENSE text is RocksDB's BSD license)
tradeoffs: Adds a dual-objective learned index (RadixSpline-based) plus an RL agent for tuning block size/error bound on top of RocksDB; extra training/tuning overhead; RL agent adds runtime complexity vs stock RocksDB.
caveats: Repo license field shows NOASSERTION on GitHub (mixed original RocksDB + new files); verified LICENSE file text is RocksDB's BSD-3-Clause. Some headline speedups (1.19x-2.21x) are versus other learned-index variants (Bourbon, TridentKV) built on RocksDB, not always stock RocksDB directly, though direct RocksDB comparisons (e.g. 81% gain, 2.21x read) are also reported explicitly.
found_via: arXiv API query all:learned+index+AND+all:LSM+AND+all:RocksDB -> arxiv.org/abs/2502.05369; code located via gh search repos "DobLIX"

name: DiaLSM
workload: db_bench FillRandom (8KB values) and full YCSB workload suite plus Sysbench OLTP, implemented atop RocksDB v8.3.2, 100M-entry dataset
claimed_speedup: Up to 2.4x higher throughput and 50% lower latency vs RocksDB in FillRandom; 94.3% fewer write stalls; 1.8x higher throughput vs ADOC; up to 8.9x on YCSB-E; 2.2x higher throughput in Sysbench OLTP on RocksDB-based RDBMS
hardware: Two AMD EPYC 7352 24-core CPUs, 256GB RAM, MZSLR3T8HBLS-00A07 NVMe SSD, CentOS 7 with ext4
tradeoffs: Shards the write-flush-compaction pipeline internally to avoid a single monolithic stall path; adds shard-management complexity and per-shard resource overhead.
caveats: Accepted to IEEE ICDE 2027; GitHub repo (DISCOS-LAB/DiaLSM) currently only contains a README stating source code 'will be available soon' -- no code to inspect yet, so tier capped at B and has_code=false despite hardware being stated. Compiler/flags not given in the paper.
found_via: arXiv API query all:LSM+AND+all:RocksDB -> arxiv.org/abs/2609.14370; repo located via gh search repos "DiaLSM"

name: KVell
workload: YCSB core workloads (uniform and Zipfian key distributions), 1024B items, 100GB(100M keys)/5TB(5B keys) synthetic datasets, plus two Nutanix write-heavy (57:41:2 write:read:scan) production workloads, 250B-1KB items.
claimed_speedup: KVell achieves throughput at least 2x that of its closest competitor (RocksDB 6.2, PebblesDB, TokuMX, or WiredTiger) on read-dominated workloads, and 5x on write-dominated workloads; tail latency an order of magnitude lower on scan-heavy workloads
hardware: Config-SSD: 32-core 2.4GHz Intel Xeon, 128GB RAM, 480GB Intel DC S3500 SSD; Config-Amazon-8NVMe: AWS i3.metal, 36x2 (72) cores at 2.3GHz, 488GB RAM, 8x1.9TB NVMe SSDs; Config-Optane: 4-core 4.2GHz Intel i7, 60GB RAM, 480GB Intel Optane 905P
tradeoffs: Shared-nothing architecture can suffer load imbalance; no in-memory sorted global index so scans are relatively weaker; designed around 4KB-atomic-write SSDs.
caveats: Peer-reviewed SOSP'19 paper states hardware in detail but compiler/flags were not found in the sections reviewed (intro, evaluation setup, IO design); repo's most recent commits look like housekeeping, core code dates to the 2019 paper.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "KVell" -> BLepers/KVell; paper PDF downloaded from repo and read directly

name: MatrixKV
workload: Random-write workload on a hybrid DRAM/NVM/SSD system using Intel Optane DC PMM, per the USENIX ATC'20 paper.
claimed_speedup: 3.6x higher random-write throughput and 5x lower 99th-percentile latency than RocksDB (also 2.6x/1.9x vs NoveLSM)
hardware: Intel Optane DC PMM (3D XPoint NVM) in a hybrid DRAM/NVM/SSD system
tradeoffs: Requires Intel Optane/PMDK-class NVM hardware to realize the reported gains; not a plain-SSD design.
caveats: Code is implemented as a diff against RocksDB v5.18.3 (not a GitHub fork, but explicitly derived, per repo instructions to `git reset --mixed` against that RocksDB commit); compiler/flags not stated on the paper abstract page viewed; repo unmaintained since 2020.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "MatrixKV" -> PDS-Lab/MatrixKV; paper page at usenix.org

name: PebblesDB
workload: db_bench-style single- and multi-threaded micro-benchmarks (50M KV pairs, 1KB values) plus a YCSB run (50M KV pairs, 1KB values, ~52GB user data) comparing PebblesDB, LevelDB, HyperLevelDB and RocksDB.
claimed_speedup: PebblesDB achieves 6x the write throughput of RocksDB, with similar read throughput and about 50% less IO (SOSP'17 peer-reviewed paper)
compiler_and_flags: Project states it 'was built, compiled, and tested with g++-4.7, g++-4.9, and g++-5' as a general build requirement; not confirmed as the exact compiler used for the cited benchmark run
tradeoffs: Write-optimized FLSM design trades away small-range-query performance on fully compacted stores; sequential-write throughput is lower than competitors.
caveats: benchmark.md does not itself state exact CPU model; the full SOSP'17 paper likely has it but was not opened in this session.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "LSM" "benchmark" language:C++ --sort stars

name: SplinterDB
workload: Insertion and point-query micro/macro-benchmarks on NVMe SSDs, per the USENIX ATC'20 paper 'SplinterDB: Closing the Bandwidth Gap for NVMe Key-Value Stores'.
claimed_speedup: 6-10x faster insertions and 2-2.6x faster point queries than RocksDB, with about 2x lower write amplification, while matching RocksDB on small range queries
tradeoffs: Project's own docs say it is not recommended for production before v1.0; gains are specifically tuned for NVMe device bandwidth characteristics.
caveats: Numbers taken from the USENIX ATC'20 paper's abstract/summary page; exact CPU model and compiler/flags used in the paper's full experiments were not verified in this session.

name: NuDB
workload: Insert N pseudo-random key/value pairs then fetch M random keys, at database sizes of 100,000 / 1,000,000 / 10,000,000 keys, per the project's own bench.cpp harness.
claimed_speedup: Sample table in repo: insert throughput 406598 vs 231937 ops/sec at 100K keys, 374330 vs 258519 at 1M keys (NuDB faster); fetch throughput 333443/337300 vs 34557/20835 ops/sec at 1M/10M keys (NuDB faster) but 325228 vs 697158 at 100K keys (NuDB slower) (numbers as printed on page)
tradeoffs: Append-only, insert-only design (no update/delete), all keys must be the same size; optimized specifically for random-read performance on SSDs, e.g. content-addressable storage.

name: LIPP (Updatable Learned Index with Precise Positions)
baseline: STX B+Tree; also beats Adaptive Radix Tree (ART), ALEX, PGM-index, BwTree, and a 2-level RMI ("Learned Index")
workload: Point lookups/inserts on four datasets (Longitudes 1B, Longlat 200M, Lognormal 190M, YCSB 200M keys) under Read-Only, Read-Heavy, Write-Heavy, Write-Only workloads, single-threaded
claimed_speedup: Up to 2.8x/6.3x/15.3x/9.8x throughput vs ALEX/PGM/Learned-Index/B+Tree on read-only workloads; 2.9x/13.5x/5.4x/3.7x vs ALEX/PGM/B+Tree/ART on read-write workloads
hardware: Intel Core i7 (4 cores, 8 threads) @ 4.0GHz, 32GB RAM, Ubuntu 18.04, single thread used
tradeoffs: No concurrency support; amortized O(log^2 N) insert cost vs B+Tree's better worst case; needs periodic subtree adjustment; benefit shrinks a lot on highly non-uniform key distributions
caveats: Single-threaded benchmarks only; gains vary strongly by dataset (as low as 1.47x vs ALEX on the highly non-uniform Longlat dataset); repo unmaintained since Feb 2022
found_via: GitHub code search 'updatable learned index' + citation from the PGM-index/ALEX literature; verified via PVLDB paper PDF (Sections 6.1-6.2)

name: ALEX (Adaptive Learned indEX)
baseline: STX B+Tree (std::map-like ordered index); also beats Adaptive Radix Tree (ART), a 2-stage RMI ("Learned Index"), and a Model-enhanced B+Tree
workload: Point lookups/inserts on 4 real datasets (longitudes, longlat, lognormal, YCSB; 200M 8-byte keys) under read-only and read-write (mixed insert) workloads, single-threaded
claimed_speedup: Up to 4.1x/2.2x/2.9x/3.0x higher throughput and 800x/15x/160x/8000x smaller index than B+Tree/Learned-Index/Model-B+Tree/ART on read-only workloads; up to 4.0x/2.7x/2.7x higher throughput and 2000x/475x/36000x smaller index vs B+Tree/Model-B+Tree/ART on read-write workloads
hardware: Intel Core i9-9900K 3.6GHz, 64GB RAM, Ubuntu Linux, single-threaded
stars_or_usage: 701 stars; used as a baseline by many follow-up learned-index papers (LIPP, CARMI, etc.)
tradeoffs: No concurrency support in the public implementation; can degrade under adversarial/skewed insert patterns without retraining; README explicitly calls it 'a near drop-in replacement for std::map'
caveats: Hardware stated in the SIGMOD'20 paper (arXiv preprint) but compiler/optimization flags not given in the accessible text; independently reused as a baseline by later peer-reviewed papers (LIPP, CARMI), which corroborate the B+Tree comparison
found_via: Starting query variation: 'in-memory learned index drop-in replacement std::map faster than B-tree'

name: ART Synchronized (Optimistic Lock Coupling / ROWEX for Adaptive Radix Tree)
baseline: Masstree (concurrent B-tree/trie hybrid key-value index) -- not one of the assignment's named baselines, recorded honestly as the incumbent the paper actually benchmarks against
workload: Concurrent lookup/insert/remove throughput at up to 20 threads on 50M random 8-byte integer keys (low contention), plus lookup/insert at 20 threads on three string datasets (genome 256K keys, Wikipedia 16M titles, URL 6.4M URLs), comparing ART synchronization variants (Optimistic Lock Coupling, ROWEX, HTM) vs Masstree
claimed_speedup: ROWEX/Optimistic Lock Coupling beat Masstree by roughly 2x on lookup/insert throughput for the genome and URL string datasets at 20 threads; Masstree is faster on the Wikipedia dataset and closes the gap with longer keys
hardware: Intel Xeon E5-2687W v3 (Haswell EP, 10 cores/20 threads), 25MB L3 cache
tradeoffs: Requires jemalloc and TBB; ROWEX needs custom epoch-based memory reclamation and is the most complex variant to implement/maintain; the paper itself notes the ART-vs-Masstree comparison is not apples-to-apples since the synchronization protocols and data structures differ
caveats: Results are mixed across datasets (Masstree wins on the Wikipedia string dataset); Masstree is not one of the assignment's named baselines; the last GitHub push (2026-05-24) is likely a housekeeping commit on an otherwise ~2015-era codebase, so treat 'active' loosely
found_via: GitHub topic search 'adaptive radix tree concurrent' -> cross-referenced against the ART synchronization DaMoN 2016 paper

name: CARMI (Cache-Aware RMI)
baseline: STX B+Tree and ALEX; also beats RMI on the SOSD benchmark platform
workload: Point lookups/inserts on 7 datasets (uniform, lognormal, YCSB, OSM, Facebook, ~10^8 keys) under read-only/write-heavy/read-heavy/write-partial/range-scan workloads, single-threaded, 100k operations per workload
claimed_speedup: Average 2.2x/1.9x speedup vs B+Tree/ALEX while using only ~0.77x the memory of B+Tree; on the SOSD platform CARMI beats all baselines with an average 1.2x speedup over the nearest competitor, RMI
hardware: AMD Ryzen 3700X 8-core CPU, 32GB RAM, Ubuntu Linux, single-threaded
tradeoffs: Read/static-friendly cost model; construction is more expensive due to a cost-based dynamic-programming search; gains shrink on already cache-friendly small datasets
caveats: Very low adoption (10 stars) and repo has not been updated since Jan 2022; numbers come from the authors' own paper, though it is peer-reviewed (PVLDB)
found_via: gh search repos 'cache aware learned index' -> embryo-labs/CARMI, cross-checked against the arXiv preprint (2103.00858)

name: PGM-index (Piecewise Geometric Model index)
baseline: 2-stage RMI (Recursive Model Index); also matches a cache-efficient B+-tree and CSS-tree at far less space
workload: Point queries on a Web Logs dataset (~715M timestamps, 8-byte keys, 128-byte payload), 10M random queries against an in-memory sorted array index
claimed_speedup: PGM-index matches the fastest B+-tree's query latency using ~10,000x less space (87 KiB vs 874 MiB) and matches the fastest CSS-tree using 83x less space (4 MiB vs 341 MiB); at matched space, PGM-index dominates a 2-stage RMI in latency
hardware: 2.3 GHz Intel Xeon Gold CPU, 192 GiB memory
stars_or_usage: 874 stars; basis for the PyGM Python wrapper, widely cited in follow-on learned-index papers
tradeoffs: Base structure targets static/append-friendly data (a dynamic variant exists but adds complexity); requires a sorted key array; the headline win vs traditional trees is space at matched latency, not a raw query-latency multiplier
caveats: VLDB'20 paper states hardware but not compiler/flags; the clear throughput/latency win over a named baseline is specifically vs RMI, while the B+-tree/CSS-tree comparisons are same-speed-less-space rather than strictly faster
found_via: GitHub topic search 'learned index' + citation chain from the LIPP and CARMI papers

name: Adaptive Radix Tree (rafaelkallis/adaptive-radix-tree)
baseline: std::map (red-black tree, libstdc++) -- the closest stdlib ordered-index analog to the assignment's B-tree baseline
workload: 1.6M sparse 64-bit keys; delete/insert/mixed/query (uniform and Zipfian) micro-benchmarks comparing art::art vs std::map vs std::unordered_map
claimed_speedup: ~1.5x-2.1x faster than std::map on delete (1.985x), insert (2.118x), mixed (1.824x), query-uniform (1.517x) and query-zipf (1.817x); slower than std::unordered_map on delete/query, roughly at parity on insert/mixed
tradeoffs: GPL-3.0 (copyleft) limits use in permissively-licensed or proprietary code; slower than std::unordered_map for pure lookups/deletes in this benchmark; only sparse-key workload shown
caveats: No compiler flags or CPU model stated for the benchmark numbers; it is the project's own micro-benchmark (uses nanobench-style harness), not an independent suite

claimed_speedup: Local-FS mode: 450 MB/s vs Kafka's 129.96 MB/s (3.5x) and Pulsar's 107 MB/s (4.2x), with 1.8ms vs Kafka's 58ms latency; S3 mode: 750 MB/s (5.8x vs Kafka)

name: Prefix Filter
workload: Space usage, false-positive rate, operation throughput at varying load, and build time for 0.94*2^28 (~252M) random 64-bit keys at false-positive rate ~2^-8, single-threaded, on an Intel Ice Lake server (PVLDB 15(7), 2022)
claimed_speedup: Overall build time faster than the vector quotient filter and cuckoo filter by 1.39-1.46x and 3.2-3.5x respectively; cuckoo filter's own insertion throughput collapses (a 27x slowdown observed) as occupancy approaches capacity, while prefix filter insertions stay fast; query throughput is comparable to (though about 52%/79% behind, for negative/positive queries) the cuckoo filter at low occupancy; far more space-efficient than the blocked Bloom filter at low target false-positive rates
compiler_and_flags: GCC 10.3.0, Ubuntu 20.04 (specific optimization flags beyond compiler version not stated in the extracted text)
hardware: Intel Xeon Gold 6336Y (Ice Lake) @ 2.40GHz, 64GiB RAM, 48KiB L1d/1.25MiB L2 per core, 36MiB shared L3
tradeoffs: Requires AVX-512 hardware for the fast path; is an incremental filter (supports insertion but the paper focuses on a fixed configured capacity); this is a mixed win, not a strict speed win across every metric.
caveats: IMPORTANT: query throughput is NOT better than the cuckoo filter in this paper's own numbers -- the cuckoo filter is faster for queries at low occupancy (by 52%/79%). Prefix filter's real advantages are build/insertion time and avoiding cuckoo filter's occupancy-dependent insertion collapse, plus much better space efficiency than the blocked Bloom filter. Repo license is Apache-2.0 per LICENSE.md though GitHub's own license detector reports NOASSERTION.
found_via: GitHub: gh api repos/FastFilter/fastfilter_cpp/readme -> Credits section -> TomerEven/Prefix-Filter; paper arXiv:2203.17139

name: Xor Filter (xor_singleheader)
workload: Single-threaded membership-test query time vs. space overhead for 10M and 100M random 64-bit keys, 25% of queried keys present, using the fastfilter_cpp bulk-insert-and-query benchmark
claimed_speedup: At 10M keys: Xor8 23ns/query (9.8 bits/key) vs Bloom12 40ns (12.0 bits/key) and Cuckoo12 31ns (12.8 bits/key); Xor16 27ns (19.7 bits/key) vs Bloom16 48ns (16.0 bits/key) and Cuckoo16 32ns (17.0 bits/key). At 100M keys: Xor8 32ns vs Bloom12 58ns and Cuckoo12 38ns (Table 3, Graf & Lemire, JEA 2020)
hardware: Intel i7-6700 @ 3.4GHz (Skylake), 8MiB L3 cache
stars_or_usage: 432 stars; used in production by Databend, ntop nDPI, InfiniFlow, and CockroachDB Pebble
tradeoffs: Immutable once built (no add/remove; must know the full key set upfront); needs a strong ~64-bit hash of the input keys; construction is slower than Bloom/blocked-Bloom (~110-130ns/key vs ~10-40ns/key at 10M keys per Table 2 of the same paper); naturally compressible with gzip/zstd, unlike Bloom/cuckoo.
caveats: Numbers are from the peer-reviewed Journal of Experimental Algorithmics paper (Graf & Lemire 2020), single-threaded, one 2019-era CPU (Skylake); margin over cuckoo filter is modest (23ns vs 31ns) though clearer over Bloom filter (40-48ns). Code is in FastFilter/xor_singleheader and the benchmark harness in FastFilter/fastfilter_cpp.
found_via: GitHub: gh api repos/FastFilter/fastfilter_cpp/readme -> References section -> arXiv:2201.01174
GitHub: gh api repos/FastFilter/xor_singleheader/readme -> linked paper arXiv:1912.08258; cross-checked against FastFilter/fastfilter_cpp benchmark README

name: BuRR (Ribbon Filter)
workload: Space-overhead comparison of ribbon-filter (retrieval + AMQ) configurations against Bloom, xor, and xor+ filters at varying false-positive rates; best-paper-winning SEA 2022 evaluation (fastfilter_cpp harness)
claimed_speedup: Classic Bloom filters use 1.44*log2(1/f) bits/key (44% over the theoretical minimum); xor filters achieve ~20% overhead and xor+ ~10% for small f; BuRR (ribbon filter) achieves overheads as low as 0.1%, and even speed-optimized configurations stay below 0.5%, while described as having 'extremely low overhead and fast queries'
stars_or_usage: 52 stars; won Best Paper at SEA 2022 (20th International Symposium on Experimental Algorithms)
tradeoffs: Static/immutable retrieval structure (no keys stored, so it cannot enumerate members); construction cost scales worse than hash-table-based filters for very large n; a parallel-construction variant exists on a separate branch.
caveats: The headline space-overhead numbers come from the README and are attributed to the peer-reviewed SEA 2022 paper, but exact hardware/compiler/CPU model were not located in the README itself (would require reading the full LIPIcs paper or preprint to confirm, hence Tier B not A). Primary quantified claim is memory overhead, not raw query latency, though the paper title and abstract also claim fast queries.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos 'ribbon filter' -> lorenzhs/BuRR; cross-referenced via FastFilter binary-fuse-filter paper references [Dillinger & Walzer, arXiv:2103.02515] and FastFilter/fastfilter_cpp README credits

name: Morton Filter
workload: Insertion, deletion, and lookup throughput of a Morton filter (compressed, bandwidth-optimized cuckoo filter) vs. the reference cuckoo filter implementation from Fan et al., as reported in the VLDB 2018 paper
claimed_speedup: Insertion, deletion, and lookup throughputs up to 15.5x, 1.3x, and 2.5x higher than a cuckoo filter respectively, while also using fewer bits per item than a Bloom filter below ~1-3% target false-positive rate
compiler_and_flags: g++ (project recommends g++ 5.4; notes a performance regression in GCC 8.x as of March 2019)
stars_or_usage: 90 stars; developed at AMD Research, published at VLDB 2018 with an extended version in the VLDB Journal (2019)
tradeoffs: Supports self-resizing (grow capacity without a backing structure) unlike vanilla cuckoo filters; requires only a multiple-of-two bucket count rather than a power of two; author explicitly labels the code 'academic-style prototype', not hardened for production.
caveats: The 15.5x/1.3x/2.5x figures are stated in the README, sourced from the authors' own peer-reviewed VLDB paper; exact CPU model and compiler flags used for those specific figures were not confirmed from the README alone (paper PDF was not deep-read for the hardware section), so capped at Tier B. Repo has had no commits in ~5 years.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos 'morton filter' -> AMDComputeLibraries/morton_filter

name: SuRF (Succinct Range Filter)
workload: RocksDB replacement of its Bloom filters with SuRF on a synthetic 100GB time-series dataset (2K simulated sensors, 128-bit keys); end-to-end open-range, closed-range, and worst-case (all-missing-key) point query throughput, SIGMOD 2018 Best Paper
claimed_speedup: Open-range (no upper bound) queries 1.5x faster and closed-range (with upper bound) queries up to 5x faster than RocksDB's original Bloom filter, at equal filter size; but for the worst-case point-query workload (no query keys exist) RocksDB is up to 40% SLOWER using SuRF instead of Bloom filters, because SuRF has a higher false-positive rate at that size (0.2% vs 0.1%)
hardware: Intel Core i7-6770HQ CPU, 32GB RAM, Intel 540s 480GB SSD
stars_or_usage: 554 stars; SIGMOD 2018 Best Paper; evaluated as a RocksDB Bloom-filter replacement
tradeoffs: SuRF trades a higher false-positive rate for the ability to answer range queries and approximate range counts, which plain Bloom filters cannot do at all; for pure point-query, moderate-FPP workloads the paper itself says 'the Bloom filter is usually a better choice than SuRF'; construction speed is comparable to Bloom filter's.
caveats: This is a mixed/nuanced result, not a strict win: SuRF is slower (up to 40%) for point-only, all-miss workloads at equal filter size; its wins (1.5x-5x) are specifically for range queries. Compiler name/flags were not found in the excerpts read (only CPU/RAM/SSD stated), so capped at Tier B.
found_via: GitHub: gh api repos/efficient/SuRF (found via reasoning about range-filter alternatives to Bloom filter beyond the assignment's seed query); README links SIGMOD best paper

name: Vacuum Filter
workload: Positive/mixed lookup, insertion, and deletion throughput plus bits-per-item vs. target false-positive rate, 64-bit random keys, varying table occupancy 0-100%, on a DELL workstation (PVLDB 13, 2020)
claimed_speedup: Semi-sorted vacuum filter (VF-ss) is about 1.1x-1.8x faster than semi-sorted cuckoo filter (CF-ss) for positive lookups; vacuum filter has the highest insertion throughput among AMQ structures compared when table occupancy < 65%; vacuum filters use 2-5 fewer bits per item than cuckoo filter, Bloom filter, Morton filter, and counting quotient filter at the same target false-positive rate
hardware: DELL workstation, Intel Xeon E5-2687W @ 3.00GHz, 30MB L3 cache, SK-hynix SC311-S 1TB SSD
tradeoffs: Built on top of / modified from Fan et al.'s cuckoo filter code; the fast implementation is a modified cuckoo filter rather than a from-scratch design; deletion throughput is only 'similar to' cuckoo filter, not better; insertion advantage narrows and eventually loses to cuckoo/vacuum crossover above ~65% occupancy where both slow down comparably.
caveats: CPU model is stated but the paper excerpt read did not contain explicit compiler name/version or optimization flags, so capped at Tier B rather than A. This is peer reviewed (PVLDB) with code public.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos 'vacuum filter' -> wuwuz/Vacuum-Filter; paper at vldb.org/pvldb/vol13/p197-wang.pdf
